question: In its reply to question E-002040/2024, the Commission cites data from an analysis carried out in 20231 to justify a change in the protection status of wolves, referring both to the wider distribution area and the increase in wolf populations.

However, this analysis also points out that: some populations are small with fewer than 1 000 mature individuals, the threshold below which a population would be listed as ‘Vulnerable’; estimates of wolf numbers vary greatly across different countries due to the lack of a census method for counting wolves and uniform monitoring; the conservation status of wolves in many Member States is ‘unfavourable-inadequate’ or ‘unfavourable-bad’; and of the thirty nine national biogeographic assessments reported in the previous six-year reporting period (2013-2018) sixteen were ‘unfavourable-inadequate’, three were ‘unfavourable-bad’ and two were unknown.
In view of the above: 1.
Why didn’t the Commission wait for the next six-year report before presenting its proposal, which is not based on accurate population data?
Why does the Commission buy into the alleged positive trend, which indicates that the conservation status of wolves is favourable?
Why has the Commission not taken precautions and focused its efforts on damage prevention?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.1.2025) The analysis of the wolf situation published in December 2023 by the Commission1 considered the best available data including the conservation status assessments reported by Member States under Article 17 of the Habitats Directive2; the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List assessments; as well as updated information on wolf numbers in the EU.

This analysis showed that the conservation status of the wolf in Europe has significantly recovered over the last decades and that the general trends in population and range were still improving. The Commission therefore considered, with that information at hand, that waiting for the next reports to be submitted under Article 17 of the Habitats Directive was not necessary.

Generally increasing trends of both population and range of wolves in Europe have been confirmed by the latest available data, recently published by the Commission3. A change of the protection status of the wolf in the Habitats Directive4 would not remove the obligation for Member States to reach or maintain good conservation status of wolf populations.
It will rather provide additional flexibility to the Member States that need it, without obliging other Member States to change the protection status of the wolf at national level.

Irrespective of any change in the legal protection status of the wolf, the Commission will continue to promote and support, through EU funding instruments, the design and implementation of appropriate coexistence solutions, including measures to prevent and reduce livestock depredations by protected wildlife species5.
